t: Maximum Price to Fill a Bag — Fractional Knapsack
o: Items are divisible: taking a fraction f of item i yields price_i*f for weight_i*f. Maximize total price filling exactly capacity; if total weight of all items is less than capacity, filling is impossible (-1). This is the classic fractional knapsack, solved greedily: always take the item with the highest price-per-unit-weight first. Example 1: item densities are 50 and 1.25, so take all of item 1 (weight 1, price 50) then 4 units of item 2 (price 5) → 55. Example 2: total weight 30 < 50 → -1. With up to 1e5 items, sorting dominates the runtime.
k: Greedy exchange argument: replacing any lower-density mass in an optimal solution with higher-density mass never decreases value.
First check feasibility: sum of weights must be at least capacity.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy by density after sorting
a.i: Sort items by price/weight descending. Walk through, taking min(remaining capacity, weight) of each item and adding proportionally priced value, until capacity is filled. Because items are freely divisible, the greedy choice is optimal by a standard exchange argument.
s: Sort items by price/weight in descending order.
Take greedily: for each item add price * taken/weight and reduce capacity; stop at capacity 0.
a.t: O(m log m) — sorting m items dominates the linear fill pass
a.sp: O(1) extra (or O(m) depending on sort) — in-place sort and scalars

w: Present the greedy plus the feasibility pre-check. Pitfalls: integer division when comparing densities (compare as doubles or cross-multiply), forgetting the -1 case, and overflow of total weight (up to 1e9) in fixed-width languages. Follow-up: if items were indivisible this becomes 0/1 knapsack needing DP.
